headline_marked: [[Early NVIDIA advisor discovers]] he's owed a billion dollars in stock from 1993 options
headline: Early NVIDIA advisor discovers he's owed a billion dollars in stock from 1993 options
summary: An early NVIDIA advisor from 1993 recently uncovered a discrepancy in his stock option vesting schedule, potentially entitling him to an additional 4.5 million shares, now valued at approximately one billion dollars.
details: An early technical advisor to NVIDIA, who joined in 1993, recently discovered he is owed approximately one billion dollars in stock. He was granted 25,000 options in September 1993, intended to vest over one year.

The advisor, who had previously worked with NVIDIA co-founder Curtis Priem, contributed significantly to early texture mapping techniques. His biquadratic texture mapping implementation caught the attention of the NVIDIA founders.

He casually worked with Curtis on porting his texture mapping to their hardware and wrote code for an Intel-sponsored VR demo. However, when NVIDIA's NV1 shipped in 1995, Microsoft's DirectX did not support quadratic texture mapping, severely impacting NVIDIA's early finances and leading to layoffs.
In April 1996, NVIDIA's CFO informed him that 15,625 shares had vested, which he exercised and subsequently forgot about. He had expatriated to Tonga by then, working on internet startup schemes.

Fast-forward to 2024, prompted by NVIDIA's prominence, he reviewed his old documents. He found that his option agreement specified a one-year vesting schedule, not the four-year schedule implied by the 1996 letter, which would have meant all 25,000 shares should have vested.
Due to numerous stock splits (a cumulative 480x), his missing 9,375 shares now amount to 4,500,000 shares. He engaged formidable attorneys to explore the issue with NVIDIA.

After about a year of correspondence between attorneys, NVIDIA did not dispute the authenticity of the option agreement but asserted the claims were time-barred. NVIDIA's counsel, Cooley, essentially responded with "so sue us."

Despite the clear contractual discrepancy, the advisor and his attorneys concluded that the statute of limitations was against them. The thirty-odd years that had passed made it unlikely they would succeed past a motion to dismiss, serving as a cautionary tale about contractual obligations.
